body:
Why departmental response is different

A government department may hold citizens' personal information, deliver essential services or connect to shared information systems. An incident may therefore affect many people rather than a single account holder. Its response must protect the system, maintain lawful public services and preserve records for possible technical or criminal investigation.

Individual employees are responsible for promptly reporting unusual activity through their department's authorised channels. Technical decisions should normally be taken by the designated information-technology or security personnel, not through independent experimentation by an untrained employee.

Recognising a possible departmental incident

Warning signs may include unexpected account activity, unexplained changes to records, loss of access to important files, suspicious messages sent from an official account or an unusual interruption of a government service. These are reasons to report and verify the problem; they do not automatically prove malicious activity.

For example, if a taluka office finds that an authorised user can no longer access a service application, the office should inform its designated support and security staff. The responsible team can distinguish routine technical failure from a security incident and take appropriate action.

The basic response sequence

  1. Identify and record. Note what happened, when it was noticed, which service or account appears affected and who first observed it. Report observable facts without guessing the attacker's identity.
  2. Escalate internally. Notify the designated information-technology team, information-security officer or Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), as provided by departmental procedure. The supervisor and responsible technical team should be informed without avoidable delay.
  3. Contain through authorised action. The technical team may restrict affected access or isolate an affected system where appropriate. The objective is to prevent further harm without unnecessarily disrupting other services or destroying relevant records.
  4. Preserve information. Retain relevant alerts, records and communications in accordance with departmental instructions. Employees should not casually erase files, reset affected devices or circulate sensitive records through personal messaging accounts.
  5. Make required external reports. The designated authority should assess whether the incident falls within CERT-In's reporting directions and whether a suspected offence must also be brought to the police.
  6. Restore services safely. Authorised personnel should verify that affected services can resume appropriately, communicate necessary information to users and record the action taken.

These activities may overlap. For example, an institution may need to preserve records and report the incident while its technical team is still examining the cause.

CERT-In and the 6-hour reporting direction

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) is the national agency for cyber incident response under section 70B of the Information Technology Act, 2000. It operates under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY).

CERT-In's directions dated 28 April 2022 require specified categories of entities, including service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government organisations, to report the cyber incidents listed in Annexure I, including unauthorised access, malware attacks and data breaches, within 6 hours of noticing them or being brought to notice about them.

The 6-hour requirement concerns the specified entities and reportable incidents covered by CERT-In's directions. It is not a general rule requiring every individual citizen to report every suspicious message within 6 hours. It is also a reporting deadline, not a requirement that the entire incident be resolved within 6 hours.

Departments should therefore have clear internal escalation arrangements so that a reportable incident reaches the responsible officer promptly. Delay within the organisation may interfere with compliance even when a junior employee reported the problem to a colleague.

Technical incident reporting and criminal reporting

An incident may require technical coordination, police investigation or both. CERT-In's function is to collect and analyse information about cyber incidents, issue alerts and advisories, and coordinate response. The police investigate suspected criminal offences under the applicable law.

Suppose a public-service application becomes unavailable following suspicious activity. The responsible technical officials may need to inform CERT-In if the incident falls within the reporting directions. If evidence also suggests unlawful access or fraud, the appropriate police authority may need to be informed. Neither action automatically replaces the other.

Preparedness and staff training

Incident response improves when employees know whom to contact, what information to record and which actions require technical authorisation. A departmental reporting arrangement should reduce confusion and support timely decisions.

Cyber Surakshit Bharat, launched by MeitY on 19 January 2018 with the National e-Governance Division and industry partners, was designed to strengthen awareness and capacity among government CISOs and frontline information-technology personnel. Its guiding principles are Awareness, Education and Enablement.

This initiative is a training and preparedness programme. It is not the national cybercrime helpline, a police investigation agency or a replacement for CERT-In.

Prelims focus

  • CERT-In is India's national cyber incident-response agency under IT Act section 70B.
  • CERT-In operates under MeitY.
  • CERT-In's directions are dated 28 April 2022.
  • The specified entities must report Annexure I incidents within 6 hours of noticing or being informed about them.
  • Cyber Surakshit Bharat was launched in 2018 for government cybersecurity awareness and capacity building.
  • Trap: CERT-In reporting does not replace the police investigation of a suspected crime.

[Sources: CERT-In, Directions under section 70B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, dated 28 April 2022, pp. 1-3 and Annexure I, cert-in.org.in; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, MeitY Launches Cyber Surakshit Bharat to Strengthen Cybersecurity, 19 January 2018, programme objectives and principles; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, National Cyber Security Policy, 2013, Preamble, paragraphs 5-7. Official online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Prompt internal escalation allows authorised containment and timely statutory reporting.

title: Cyber Incident Response in Government Departments and Public Institutions

body:
Why different institutions have different responsibilities

India's cybersecurity framework involves several institutions because protecting computer systems, investigating crimes and safeguarding important national infrastructure are different functions. The correct institution depends on the nature of the problem.

A fraud against a citizen requires a criminal-reporting and law-enforcement response. A serious technical incident in a government network may require CERT-In coordination. A threat to nationally important information infrastructure may require the specialised role of the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre.

The principal national and state institutions

InstitutionAdministrative connectionCore function
CERT-InMinistry of Electronics and Information TechnologyNational cyber incident response, alerts, advisories and technical coordination
I4CMinistry of Home AffairsNational coordination against cybercrime and support for reporting and law-enforcement cooperation
NCIIPCNational Technical Research OrganisationNational nodal agency for protection of critical information infrastructure
State and Union Territory policeRespective law-enforcement administrationsCybercrime complaints, investigation and related criminal-law action
Gujarat Security Operations CenterDirectorate of ICT and e-Governance, Gujarat Department of Science and TechnologyMonitoring and protection of important Gujarat government information systems

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre: I4C

I4C stands for Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre. It functions within the Ministry of Home Affairs framework for coordinating the response to cybercrime.

The I4C scheme was approved on 5 October 2018. I4C became an attached office of the Ministry of Home Affairs on 1 July 2024. These dates refer to different stages of its institutional development and should not be confused.

I4C supports coordination among law-enforcement agencies, national cybercrime reporting arrangements and measures addressing financial cyber fraud. The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and CFCFRMS operate within this wider national response framework.

It is important to distinguish coordination from investigation. I4C helps connect information and institutions, while the police authorities concerned carry out criminal investigations under law.

CERT-In and NCIIPC are not the same body

CERT-In is responsible for national cyber incident-response functions under section 70B of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Its functions include incident-information analysis, advisories, alerts and coordination of technical response.

NCIIPC stands for National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre. The Central Government designated it as the national nodal agency for critical information infrastructure protection under section 70A through a notification dated 16 January 2014. It is an organisation under the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO).

The 2 institutions may have related security concerns, but their principal statutory roles differ. NCIIPC concentrates on the protection of critical information infrastructure. CERT-In has the broader national incident-response role.

70A corresponds to NCIIPC and critical information infrastructure protection. 70B corresponds to CERT-In and cyber incident response.

Police powers and the role of the states

Police and Public Order are State subjects under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India. Consequently, State and Union Territory law-enforcement agencies are primarily responsible for preventing, detecting and investigating crimes, including cybercrimes, and for pursuing cases through the criminal justice system.

The Central Government supports these functions through coordination, advisories, financial assistance and capacity-building measures. This explains why a national cybercrime reporting portal and state police investigation can operate together without being the same institution.

Gujarat's cybercrime and cybersecurity arrangements

Gujarat has a State Cyber Crime Cell associated with CID Crime, Gandhinagar, within its police framework. Cybercrime police units deal with complaints and investigations concerning suspected online offences. Citizens may use the national reporting portal or approach the appropriate police authority.

Gujarat also has a different institution: the Gujarat Security Operations Center (GSOC). According to the Gujarat Department of Science and Technology, it was established in May 2022 under the Directorate of ICT and e-Governance.

GSOC monitors cybersecurity concerns affecting important Government of Gujarat information infrastructure hosted at the Gujarat State Data Center (GSDC), Gandhinagar. It works with relevant stakeholders and national agencies, including CERT-In and NCIIPC.

These Gujarat institutions illustrate a general distinction. The police address suspected offences; GSOC focuses on the security of government information systems. A serious incident may require cooperation between technical personnel and law-enforcement authorities.

Choosing the relevant institution

For a citizen reporting an unauthorised bank transfer, the immediate relevant channels are the bank, 1930 and the cybercrime-reporting or police system. For a reportable technical incident affecting a government department, the department's responsible personnel may need to contact CERT-In. For matters involving nationally critical information infrastructure, NCIIPC has a specialised protective role.

No single institution replaces all the others. Cybersecurity requires cooperation because crime prevention, technical response, criminal investigation and protection of essential services are connected but distinct tasks.

Prelims focus

  • I4C is under the Ministry of Home Affairs; its scheme was approved in 2018 and it became an attached office in 2024.
  • CERT-In is under MeitY and is linked to IT Act section 70B.
  • NCIIPC is under NTRO and was designated under IT Act section 70A in 2014.
  • State and Union Territory police investigate cybercrimes under applicable law.
  • Gujarat Security Operations Center was established in May 2022 and protects important Gujarat government information systems.
  • Trap: I4C, CERT-In, NCIIPC and GSOC do not have identical functions.

[Sources: Ministry of Home Affairs, Cyber and Information Security Division, Overview about I4C, mha.gov.in; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Home Affairs, National Cybercrime Response Mechanism, 22 July 2026; CERT-In, Directions under IT Act section 70B(6), 28 April 2022, p. 1; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Gazette of India notification S.O. 18(E), 16 January 2014, designation of NCIIPC; Government of Gujarat, Department of Science and Technology, Projects and Initiatives, Gujarat Security Operations Center and Gujarat State Data Centre sections, website updated 27 October 2026; Gujarat Department of Science and Technology, State IT policy document, Cyber Crime section concerning CID Crime. Official online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]
